```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup}
library(missBART)
```

**missBART** fits selection models to multivariate responses whose missing
values may be *missing not at random* (MNAR): whether a value is recorded can
depend on the value itself. The responses follow a multivariate BART model.
The missingness indicators follow either

* a multivariate probit regression on the covariates and the responses
  (`missBART1()`), or
* a multivariate probit BART model on the covariates and the responses
  (`missBART2()`).

The missing responses are imputed while the model is fitted. `mvBART()` fits
the multivariate BART model on its own to complete responses. The models are
described in Goh, Soh, Parnell and Murphy (2024),
[arXiv:2412.14946](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14946).

## Simulated data

We simulate two correlated responses from five covariates, and then delete
values with a probability that increases with the value itself.

```{r}
set.seed(2024)
n <- 400
x <- matrix(runif(n * 5), ncol = 5)
f <- cbind(10 * sin(pi * x[, 1] * x[, 2]) + 20 * (x[, 3] - 0.5)^2 + 10 * x[, 4] + 5 * x[, 5],
           5 * x[, 1] - 8 * x[, 2]^2 + 3 * x[, 3])
y_true <- f + matrix(rnorm(2 * n), ncol = 2) %*% chol(matrix(c(1, 0.6, 0.6, 1), 2))

y <- y_true
y[runif(n) < pnorm(-1 + 1.2 * scale(y_true[, 1])), 1] <- NA
y[runif(n) < pnorm(-1 + 1.2 * scale(y_true[, 2])), 2] <- NA
colMeans(is.na(y))
```

The observed values are a biased sample: the missing values are larger on
average than the observed ones.

```{r}
rbind(observed = colMeans(y, na.rm = TRUE),
      missing = c(mean(y_true[is.na(y[, 1]), 1]), mean(y_true[is.na(y[, 2]), 2])))
```

## missBART1: probit regression for the missingness

The chains here are short so that the vignette builds quickly; use the
defaults, or longer chains, for real analyses.

```{r}
fit1 <- missBART1(x, y, n_trees = 50, burn = 500, iters = 500, thin = 1,
                  mice_impute = FALSE, show_progress = FALSE)
fit1
```

`imputed_values()` summarises the posterior of every missing response, and
`completed_data()` fills in their posterior means.

```{r}
imp1 <- imputed_values(fit1)
head(imp1)
truth <- y_true[fit1$missing_index]
plot(truth, imp1$mean, xlab = "True value", ylab = "Posterior mean imputation",
     col = factor(imp1$column), pch = 19, cex = 0.6)
abline(0, 1)
```

The probit coefficients describe the missingness mechanism. Each column refers
to the missingness of one response, and a positive coefficient makes that
response more likely to be *observed*. Posterior intervals for the rows `Y1`
and `Y2` that exclude zero indicate MNAR data. (With `scale = TRUE` the
coefficients refer to covariates and responses scaled to `[-0.5, 0.5]`.)

```{r}
round(coef(fit1), 2)
```

## missBART2: probit BART for the missingness

```{r}
fit2 <- missBART2(x, y, n_reg_trees = 50, n_class_trees = 20, burn = 500, iters = 500,
                  thin = 1, mice_impute = FALSE, show_progress = FALSE)
fit2
```

There are no coefficients to inspect here. Instead, `varimp()` reports how
often each predictor is used in the splitting rules of the missingness trees.
Splits concentrated on the responses point towards MNAR data.

```{r}
barplot(varimp(fit2), ylab = "Proportion of splitting rules")
```

## Comparison with ignoring the missingness

Fitting multivariate BART to the complete cases and predicting the incomplete
rows ignores the reason the values are missing.

```{r}
cc <- complete.cases(y)
fit0 <- mvBART(x[cc, ], y[cc, ], x_predict = x[!cc, ], n_trees = 50, burn = 500,
               iters = 500, thin = 1, show_progress = FALSE)
pred0 <- matrix(NA, n, 2)
pred0[!cc, ] <- predict(fit0)

rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))
c(complete_cases = rmse(pred0[fit1$missing_index], truth),
  missBART1 = rmse(imp1$mean, truth),
  missBART2 = rmse(imputed_values(fit2)$mean, truth))
```

## What is in a fit

A fit is a list of posterior draws, one list element per kept iteration; see
`?missBART1` for all components. For example, `y_post` holds the BART mean
function, `y_pred` posterior predictive draws, `y_impute` the imputed values
(ordered as `which(is.na(y))`), `sigma_post` the residual covariance matrix
and, if `x_predict` is supplied, `new_y_hat` and `new_y_post` the mean
function and predictive draws for new covariates.

```{r}
round(Reduce("+", fit1$sigma_post) / length(fit1$sigma_post), 2)
```
